articles.title: Bringing back the Monroe Doctrine is the ideal America First strategy
articles.summary: Trump's Monroe Doctrine revival deploys troops to Panama and MQ-9 Reaper drones to counter threats across the Western Hemisphere's key regions.
articles.body: More than 200 years ago, President James Monroe established a simple principle: the security of the United States is directly tied to the security of the Western Hemisphere. Today, that principle is just as vital. With communist China expanding its influence throughout Latin America and transnational criminal organizations threatening American communities, it is time to reaffirm the Monroe Doctrine and put American interests first in our own hemisphere. President Donald Trump's efforts to expand military training and security cooperation with Latin American partners represent the exact forward-thinking America First policies our national security demands. Deploying elements of the 10th Mountain Division to Panama for jungle training and joint exercises marks an important step toward strengthening the Shield of the Americas initiative. By strengthening our regional allies, we take the fight to criminal organizations before their operations reach American communities. Providing partners with the training, equipment and intelligence they need helps them dismantle drug-trafficking networks, disrupt smuggling routes and stop deadly drugs before reaching our borders. This protects American interests while allowing allies to take the lead in securing their own countries. PENTAGON SENDS HUNDREDS OF ARMY TROOPS TO LATIN AMERICA FOR TRAINING AS DRUG-TRAFFICKING CAMPAIGN EXPANDS The Trump administration is also expanding regional intelligence capabilities by shifting MQ-9 Reaper drones from U.S. Africa Command to U.S. Southern Command. Supporting operations in Colombia and Ecuador, these aircraft deliver critical surveillance to track trafficking networks across remote jungles, borders and maritime routes. Combined with greater intelligence sharing and coordinated operations, these efforts help dismantle criminal networks at the source. However, drug trafficking is only one part of the threat. During a recent congressional delegation trip to Ecuador, Peru and Colombia, we saw firsthand the growing influence of communist China. Beijing has spent years expanding its economic and strategic footprint through investments in ports, mining operations, critical infrastructure and key industries. These investments are not simply about trade; they give China leverage over regional economies, access to critical resources and influence over historically reliable American partners. TRUMP ADMIN'S LIST OF US-DESIGNATED 'FOREIGN TERRORIST' GROUPS IN LATIN AMERICA EXPANDS TO 21 One of the clearest examples is the Port of Chancay in Peru. Built and operated by Chinese state-owned COSCO, this deep-water port has the capacity to transform trade between South America and Asia. While increased trade benefits Peru's economy, China's control of critical infrastructure raises serious security concerns regarding intelligence collection, logistical support or future military use. The United States cannot stand by while our greatest strategic competitor establishes a foothold in our backyard. While in Peru, our delegation met with U.S. Ambassador Bernie Navarro, who is actively strengthening this crucial partnership. Navarro is demonstrating the value of strong American diplomatic leadership. His recent coordination with Peruvian defense officials and Southern Command commander General Francis Donovan to combat narcoterrorist organizations, including those in the Valle de los Ríos Apurímac, Ene y Mantaro (Valley of the Apurímac, Ene and Mantaro rivers), also known as the VRAEM region, is the results-driven engagement we need. RUBIO WARNS CHINA AFTER PANAMA SHIP DETENTIONS, CALLS HEMISPHERE SOVEREIGNTY 'NON-NEGOTIABLE' These efforts reinforce a central truth: a strong American presence in the hemisphere does not require us to act alone. It requires working with willing partners who share our interest in combating criminal networks, protecting sovereignty and preventing hostile foreign powers from gaining strategic influence. That is why renewing our commitment to the Monroe Doctrine is critical. The Western Hemisphere cannot be treated as a secondary priority while China expands its influence and criminal organizations exploit weak institutions and porous borders. The threats emerging from Latin America directly affect American national security, our economy and the safety of our communities. WALTZ WARNS OF CHINESE, RUSSIAN-FUELED ‘NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT’ LOOMING CLOSE TO US SHORES As a member of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs, I believe our foreign policy and assistance must produce tangible benefits for the American people. Our embassies, security partnerships and diplomatic resources must focus on advancing American interests, countering Chinese influence and helping allies confront shared threats. That also means demanding accountability. Taxpayers deserve to know their dollars are spent effectively, that partners contribute their fair share and that investments deliver measurable results. We should cut wasteful programs and direct resources toward initiatives that strengthen national security. articles.title: We represent Wyoming — California is waging war on our coal, we're going to keep mining

President Trump backed it this summer with $75 million through the Defense Production Act. Far-left politicians in Sacramento responded to this historical investment with a new layer of environmental review written to stall the project until its investors give up. California politicians didn’t like the result — so they changed the rules. AMERICAN BUSINESSES AREN’T ALLOWED TO BUILD. The governor further revealed his extreme priorities that same day when he vetoed another bill to speed up the hiring of auditors for California’s high-speed rail project. American coal offers the United States an abundance of affordable, reliable power here at home and enhanced diplomatic leverage abroad. Wyoming will not sit quietly while California politicians attempt to shut our energy producers out of global markets. Wyoming has made clear that we will use every tool at our disposal, including legal action, to defend our state and its industries. articles.title: Pulaku: The two faces of Nigeria’s vigilantes
articles.summary: Allegations of torture and abuse shadow a Fulani-led vigilante group despite its role in clamping down on kidnappers.
articles.body:
Adamawa State, Nigeria - The night they came for Daniel Musa*, the dogs were barking.

At about 11:30 pm on May 23, 2023, Musa looked out of a window overlooking the gate of his home in Adamawa State, northeastern Nigeria.

The intruders wore all black, like the night. Their faces were uncovered.

Musa, 49, usually left his dogs loose in the compound at night. But the men who had climbed over the fence drove them back into their cage and locked it, clearing a path to the house.

Then they broke the padlock on a smaller gate and moved towards the main door. There, they began trying to force it open with a digger.

Musa, a local pastor, knew they were coming in. Rather than wait for them to break down the door, he opened it himself; he didn’t want any trouble.

He had already told his wife and his then 13-year-old daughter to stay in their bedroom. The men entered his home, pointed a gun at him, and ordered him to sit on the floor.

One went into his bedroom and took money and phones. Another walked to the fridge and helped himself to bread, milk, and water.

Then, at gunpoint, they led Musa out of his home; he did not struggle. He feared that if they did not take him, they might take his wife or daughter instead.

For six hours, Musa walked blindfolded with his captors through bushland, crossing shallow streams until they reached the mountains. There, he heard the familiar voice of his neighbour and discovered he had also been abducted.

He would remain in captivity for three days.

By then, negotiations with his relatives over ransom were under way. The kidnappers demanded 15 million naira (about $11,256 at the time) for his release. But after contacting Musa's family members, they switched off their phones. The family could only reach them when the kidnappers chose to make contact, leaving them unable to negotiate a lower ransom.

Musa, whose name has been changed to protect his identity, says he remained blindfolded throughout his captivity. His only drinking water came from a river, and even then, his captors allowed him just a few sips at a time, whenever they chose.

The captives, still blindfolded, were warned by their abductors that if they detected police officers or vigilantes approaching, they would kill their hostages before attempting to escape.

At about 4am on Friday, gunfire erupted.

For roughly 15 minutes, shots rang out around the camp.

Musa lay on the rocky ground between two other captives, urging them not to move. They could hear voices approaching but had no way of knowing whether they belonged to their abductors or the people trying to rescue them. Were the kidnappers returning? Had the security forces found them? Or were they about to be killed, as their captors had threatened?

“We were confused. We didn’t know who was coming, so I told the others not to move,” he said.

The voices told them not to be afraid, as they removed their blindfolds. Several men stood before them; he can’t recall how many, all dressed in olive-green uniforms.

They belonged to Pulaku, a predominantly Fulani vigilante organisation fighting kidnapping and cattle rustling in northeastern Nigeria. Musa had heard of the group, but this was his first encounter with its members.

The kidnappers had fled, leaving behind food, phones and other belongings. Musa recalled that the rescuers also discovered what appeared to be a national identity card belonging to one of the suspects.

The captives then made their way down the mountain with their rescuers before the police took them to headquarters in Yola, the Adamawa State capital. There, Musa was reunited with his wife and daughter.

He recalls being filled with joy when he saw them again. He credits Pulaku with making that reunion possible.

“They saved my life,” says Musa. His church would later present Pulaku with an award, recognising its work in the community.

But the group’s growing role in fighting kidnapping has also brought the organisation under scrutiny. While some residents credit its members with saving lives, others accuse them of serious abuses. One man says they held him for more than two months and beat him so badly that he lost consciousness.

The two accounts reveal the uneasy place occupied by armed community vigilantes in a region where formal security forces have struggled to contain kidnapping and cattle rustling.

articles.title: Serbia’s snap election: What’s at stake and can students unseat Vucic?
articles.summary: A snap parliamentary vote on October 25 will determine whether a student-led group can loosen Vucic’s grip on power.
articles.body:
Serbia will hold a snap parliamentary election on October 25 .

The vote is seen as a test of whether President Aleksandar Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) can extend its 14-year grip on power and stave off a student-led movement born out of mass anti-government protests.

In November 2024, the collapse of a concrete canopy at a railway station in Novi Sad killed 16 people. What began as demands for accountability over the disaster grew into a nationwide movement against alleged corruption and the government’s handling of the tragedy.

Students emerged as the movement’s driving force, organising some of Serbia’s biggest demonstrations since the overthrow of Slobodan Milosevic. Their campaign has channelled deep frustration with the SNS, which has governed since 2012, and with a conventional opposition seen as fragmented and ineffective.

The parliamentary election was not due until late 2027. But Vucic resigned from the presidency in September, ahead of the end of his second and final constitutional term, and is leading the SNS campaign for prime minister. The manoeuvre has made the parliamentary contest central to his effort to retain political power before a separate presidential election must be held.

The main challenger is the student-backed Student List–Students Win (Studentska lista–Studenti pobeduju), which brings together candidates with little or no previous political experience, including academics, teachers and other professionals.

It is campaigning on restoring the rule of law, ending corruption and rebuilding institutions, rather than focusing on divisive questions such as Kosovo, European Union membership or relations with Russia.

“The political dynamic has changed from the ground up,” Jelena Vasiljevic, a senior research associate at the University of Belgrade’s Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory, told Al Jazeera.

Young people, long considered the country’s most politically disengaged group, have become the core of its largest social mobilisation in decades, she said.

Some opposition parties have chosen not to run and instead support the student list.

Others are contesting the election but face the prospect of failing to clear the threshold for parliament. As a result, many see the vote as not simply a contest between parties, but a referendum on whether the SNS system should continue.

The outcome will shape whether Serbia attempts to reset institutions that critics say have been hollowed out by years of party control. The SNS rejects allegations of abuse and corruption, but its opponents and rights groups accuse it of putting pressure on independent media, electoral malpractice and using state resources to maintain power.

For Vasiljevic, turnout will be decisive. The SNS retains a disciplined core electorate, supported by a clientelist model of government, in which goods and services are exchanged for political support, she said. The student list must not only unite opposition-minded voters but also mobilise habitual non-voters and the undecided.

A student list breakthrough would also remake the opposition.

Vasiljevic said parliament could contain a large group of politically inexperienced and ideologically diverse student-backed politicians, while traditional opposition parties could be greatly reduced. The result may therefore start a wider reorganisation of Serbia’s political landscape, regardless of who forms the government.

But winning power would be only the beginning.

Srdan Majstorovic, chair of the governing board of the European Policy Centre, said a new government would face the far harder task of rebuilding a democratic system after what he described as 14 years of systematic damage to institutions, the rule of law and public trust, compounded by deep social divisions and rampant corruption.

After years of what critics call a captured-state system, he said, Serbia would need a broad reset of its democratic governance.

Serbia’s stalled EU path is a part of the backdrop.

Majstorovic said progress has been blocked by concerns over the rule of law, Serbia’s limited alignment with EU sanctions, including those against Russia, and the stalled normalisation process with Kosovo.

A change in government would not automatically transform foreign policy, he said.

The student movement has avoided detailed commitments, instead treading carefully to unite left, centre and right-leaning voters.

But Majstorovic said democratic reform, judicial independence, free media and tackling corruption could renew cooperation with Brussels and revive the accession process.

Igor Bandovic, director of the Belgrade Centre for Security Policy, said foreign policy remained the biggest unknown in the student list’s programme. Its candidates have taken a hard line on Kosovo, proposed reviewing agreements reached under EU auspices and floated a referendum on EU membership within six months of taking office. They have also signalled continuity in relations with Russia.

Bandovic said a new government would probably face more immediate domestic priorities and the constraints of the Balkans’ security environment. But a referendum on EU membership could slow or halt accession further. If the SNS stays in power, he expects further deterioration in relations with Brussels.

Bandovic said Moscow has offered explicit support to the government, portraying the protests as a Western-backed “colour revolution”. The United States Congress has voiced concern about democratic standards and Serbia’s ties with Russia, while the US administration has been more restrained.

China, which has commercial interests in Serbia, has avoided public comment but is likely to prefer continuity.

Voters will elect all 250 members of the National Assembly in a single nationwide constituency.

One ballot is cast for a party or coalition list, with seats allocated proportionally.

Electoral lists generally need at least 3 percent of votes to enter parliament, while recognised minority lists are exempt from the threshold.

The list or coalition able to command a majority in the 250-seat assembly will form a government.

But with the result expected to be close and the campaign taking place amid deep mistrust, the legitimacy of the process may prove as consequential as the final seat count.

Polls will close on Sunday at 8pm local time. Preliminary results are expected about two hours later.

articles.title: In this border town, a library is trying to preserve a 125-year-old bond between the US and Canada
articles.summary: The Haskell Free Library straddles the border between Vermont and Canada, with a black line on its floor to mark the precise international border. Its new entrance is a symbol of strained relations between the countries.
articles.body: In this border town of about 700 people, you can’t separate the United States and Canada — regardless of politics. Driving its streets, two things stand out: a downhill funnel to the US-Canada border checkpoint, and a uniquely ornate library that for more than a century has embodied the longstanding bond between the two neighboring allies. The Haskell Free Library and Opera House opened in 1901 with the US-Canada border running right through the middle of the building, represented by a black line on the floor. Some parts of the library are in Vermont while others are in Quebec, although visitors can use both sides. On the ground floor there are books in English and French while upstairs there’s a theater where people in the audience can sit in the US with their feet in Canada. “I used to go to the library there when I was a kid all the time,” Derby Line resident Janice Beadle told CNN. She said she’s lived on this border for 72 years and when she thinks about the changes to the library she’s “just angry.” The library was intentionally built on the border to foster better understanding across both sides. For more than a century, Canadians could use the library’s front door on the US side without passing through an official international border crossing. Until now. Last year the Trump administration prompted the library to build a separate entrance on the Canadian side. It was completed in June. So as the library celebrates its 125th anniversary this month, it will do so with two official entrances – one for each country. “I kind of thought, ‘how asinine,’” local resident Sharon Campbell told CNN. She shares a unique characteristic with the library in that the US-Canada border also runs through the middle of the home she shares with her husband — an inescapable dynamic in this unusual town. “What are they gonna do next? Put a Border Patrol guy inside to make sure who’s from America?” she lamented. “It’s just a little too far.” The new entrance cost hundreds of thousands of dollars The process of adding a second entrance may have begun 10 days into President Donald Trump’s second term, when then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem visited the library. Two weeks later, Sylvie Boudreau, then president of the library’s board of trustees, said she was summoned to a meeting with a US Customs and Border Protection officer, a Border Patrol agent and a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. That’s when Boudreau learned she would preside over the end of one of the most unique bonds between the United States and Canada. She said she was told that on October 1, 2025, the sidewalk that allowed Canadian access to the unified American entrance would be closed. Instead, Canadians would have to go around to an official border checkpoint, cross into the United States there, and then come back to enter the library. “We didn’t receive anything in writing,” she told CNN. “I said, ‘I do not agree with this,’ but I know there’s nothing I can do,” Boudreau said of the meeting. To some, the change was emblematic of what would become a further distancing in already-strained US-Canada relations. And aside from ending a longstanding tradition, it created an immediate problem for Boudreau. “We have people, kids from schools around Canada, coming in buses to the library,” she said. “Most of them don’t have passports.” So, she and library leaders came up with a solution. It started as a temporary entrance out of an old emergency exit on the Canadian side of the building. To build something more permanent, would be expensive — about $650,000, the library estimated. The library appealed to the public and “it went crazy,” Boudreau said. Library officials were able to raise more than $300,000 in donations for a new entrance, she said. “It cost a fortune, but I feel safer for it,” Boudreau told CNN. “Because they are in Canada, they’re entering from Canada, and leaving back into Canada.” She resigned shortly after the entrance was completed. Her successor, Rodger Coupe, told CNN, “The intent of the library was to foster a relationship across the border, to have Americans understand Canadians and Canadians understand Americans.” But US Customs and Border Protection officials insisted the decision to end the previous arrangement was because of safety. Administration officials say the separate entrances will fight smuggling In a statement to CNN, a spokesperson for US Customs and Border Protection wrote, “Drug traffickers and smugglers were exploiting the fact that Canadians could use the US entrance without going through customs. We are ending such exploitation by criminals and protecting Americans.” CNN did not immediately find instances of drug trafficking through the library specifically, but in 2011 multiple people were involved in smuggling firearms using library facilities, according to the Department of Justice. Firearms purchased in Florida were put in small backpacks and stashed in a trashcan in the library bathroom, the department said. Another man later picked them up to transport into Quebec. He pleaded guilty to unlawful exportation of firearms from the US to Canada. More recently, in June 2026, a woman from Chile bought a Canadian and American ticket to a performance at the library, entered through Canada, and then once inside changed clothing and tried to exit into the United States, according to the Vermont US Attorney’s Office. She was arrested outside the library and pleaded guilty to illegal entry. Despite these examples, Boudreau rejected the argument that the library was the problem. She said she does see border violations from time to time but maintained they were not predominantly at the library or on its sidewalk. “It’s other places, it’s outside,” she said, adding that she reports offenses to authorities on both sides of the border. Boudreau said she was a Canadian border services agent for 20 years before retiring in 2019. A bigger issue with the library, Boudreau said, was that families and other groups on either side of the border would use it as a meeting place for reunions, potlucks or other gatherings unrelated to the facility. “That was one of the things we stopped after Covid,” she said, and it’s why the library’s website says in bold, “Family/friend reunions or cross-border visits are not allowed.” Coupe told CNN, “We’re under strict observation by both the US Border Patrol and the RCMP.” The logistical complications of a facility that straddles the border are unavoidable. “If somebody wants to mow the lawn on the Canadian side, we have to have permission,” said Evelyn Coupe, who is secretary for the board of trustees and married to Rodger, its president. But when CNN visited in September, those logistical challenges were out of sight and the library hummed with a steady stream of visitors. Some of them took advantage of the building’s premiere photo opportunity: straddling the border line with one foot in the US and the other in Canada while holding the flags of both countries. It’s the very spirit Boudreau and library leaders worked hard to preserve. “It was a pain” and “cost a fortune,” she told CNN. But she’s happy. “It was a big achievement.”

articles.title: Lula has defined Brazil’s left for decades. Can his movement survive another Bolsonaro?
articles.summary: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has a steep hill to climb after an unexpected first-round result in early October where he finished behind Flávio Bolsonaro.
articles.body: When Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva walked out of the Federal Police headquarters in Curitiba, Brazil, on November 8, 2019, hundreds of supporters were waiting for him. Many had been there, on and off, for much of the 580 days he spent behind bars, keeping vigil outside the building and calling out “good morning,” “good afternoon” and “good night” as they defended his innocence and demanded his freedom. Lula emerged into the crowd and did what he had done best throughout his political life: he gave a speech. “They didn’t imprison a man,” he declared. “They tried to kill an idea. But you can’t kill an idea.” Seven years later, Lula is Brazil’s president and is again fighting to prove that the ideas of his movement can break through the country’s deep polarization, a wave of new corruption investigations, clashes with the United States and a resurgent right sweeping through Latin America. On Sunday, he will make his fourth and likely last run for the presidency in a runoff vote against right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro who is now serving a sentence for plotting to overturn the 2022 election that he lost to Lula. Lula has a steep hill to climb after an unexpected first-round result in early October where he finished behind Flávio, with 45.16% of votes to the senator’s 47.03%. Polls now show the two running neck-and-neck in a race marked by sharply different visions for Brazil’s economy, security and place in the world. The headwinds are a lot for anyone to survive, let alone an almost 81-year-old who recently battled cancer for the second time. But as a figure whose trajectory spanned Brazil’s transition from military rule to democracy, sweeping social and economic change, and repeated political crises –– Lula is no stranger to making a comeback. A walking metamorphosis Born in 1945 to a poor family in the rural northeastern state of Pernambuco, Lula was the seventh of eight children. When he was seven, they moved to southeastern Brazil in search of a better life, where Lula worked shining shoes before becoming a metalworker in the industrial belt outside São Paulo – the birthplace of his political career. It was at those factory halls that Lula lost part of his left little finger in a workplace accident in 1964, reshaping his hand into what would become a proud symbol of his working-class identity. It’s also where he learned to command crowds after becoming a union leader in the 1970s. A natural speaker, he often addressed striking metalworkers during the final years of Brazil’s military dictatorship, when he was arrested for 31 days under the National Security Law after a 1980 strike. “He is a walking metamorphosis,” said Ricardo Kotscho, invoking the title of a famous song by rock musician Raul Seixas. The veteran Brazilian journalist and longtime friend, who served as Lula’s press secretary during his first term, met Lula in 1978, when he was assigned to cover him as he rose to prominence as a São Paulo union leader. “He made fun of my long beard,” he recalled. “’Here comes another college-educated bearded guy to pester me.’” They instantly became friends. “He is very funny and very mischievous,” Kotscho said. “He has also always been stubborn.” That stubbornness gave him the ability to articulate different sides toward a greater goal. “As a union leader, he had to learn to negotiate with the workers, the bosses, with the government, and it was a fragile situation,” Kotscho told CNN. Yet, Lula insisted he had no interest in becoming a politician. “He told me around 1978 that union leaders should stay out of politics,” Kotscho said. Two years later, Lula helped found the Workers’ Party, or PT, born out of Brazil’s labor movement. By 1989, he was running for president. He ran again in 1994 and 1998 and lost all three times. In 2002, he knew things had to change. He built alliances outside the party and its ideology, and became a more conciliatory candidate, reaching out to business leaders and softening his speech. “He even agreed to using a teleprompter, which he had always been against,” Kotscho told CNN. And finally, he won. A controversial legacy The capacity for unlikely alliances has followed Lula through politics. In 2022, he chose Geraldo Alckmin as his running mate – a former leader of the center-right PSDB, PT’s biggest rival for much of the 2000s, who had run and lost against Lula in 2006. Alckmin is again on the ticket this year. “What he does is he operates around, creating a space of convergence around him… which all sorts of contradictory forces can operate,” said John French, a historian and professor at Duke University who has studied Lula and Brazil’s labor movement for decades. “He’s very big on maintaining relationships. He’s not like somebody who cuts off ties.” That skill, along with his social programs, became a staple of his presidency. During his two terms, from 2002 to 2006, Brazil saw rising employment, a higher minimum wage and a major expansion of consumer power among poorer Brazilians, according to Brazil’s official census. Millions rose out of poverty, while more lower-income and Black Brazilians entered universities and spaces long dominated by the middle and upper classes. Brazil was also removed from the United Nations’ hunger map for the first time in 2014. Lula also raised Brazil’s profile abroad, deepening ties with developing nations while maintaining relationships with the US and Europe, and helped found the BRICS group with China, Russia, India and South Africa. During a G20 meeting in 2009, then US President Barack Obama pointed Lula out to other leaders and called him “the most popular politician on Earth.” But corruption also became a mark of his government — an awkward turn for a party that had spent its opposition years campaigning on clean government. In 2005, a vote-buying scheme known as Mensalão led to the conviction of senior PT figures and stained the party’s image. Even though Lula himself was never charged, the damage to the party’s image was severe. Under his successor, Dilma Rousseff, a much larger corruption probe that started at a gas station and was then named Lava Jato, or Operation Car Wash, uncovered a kickback scheme at state oil company Petrobras so sprawling it helped drive Rousseff’s 2016 impeachment. “Corruption became a kind of explanation for the economic crisis, and it became associated with PT,” said Luciano Da Ros, a political scientist and co-author of “Brazilian Politics on Trial.” Lula was eventually convicted of corruption and money laundering in Curitiba in 2017, in a case involving a luxury beachfront apartment prosecutors alleged builder OAS had promised him for favors. He denied wrongdoing and still sought to run that year, but the conviction made him ineligible. Brazil’s Supreme Court eventually annulled the decision in 2021, ruling the Curitiba court lacked jurisdiction, and restored his political rights – just in time for another election. He then won in 2022 by a razor-thin 1.8 points — about 2.1 million votes, the closest presidential election in Brazilian history. Although Bolsonaro lost, Bolsonarism is still very much alive and winning votes, mobilizing a growing conservative electorate fiercely opposed to Lula and the PT, which many now see as the “party of corruption.” “The fact is that corruption is cross-partisan, spread across all the major parties,” Da Ros said. “But the anti-corruption rhetoric once associated with the Brazilian left was very successfully taken by the right.” A new survival test A new corruption investigation is helping fuel the sentiment as Lula enters the 2026 campaign, leading a divided country amid a wave of institutional turmoil. The collapse of Brazilian bank Banco Master has reached across the political establishment, including the Supreme Court, just weeks before the vote. Justice Alexandre de Moraes — who battled constantly with Bolsonaro during his government and later oversaw the investigations that convicted him — is now facing questions over alleged ties to the bank’s president. Moraes has denied the allegations. CNN has reached out to him for comment. Portrayed as a Lula ally for his clashes with Bolsonaro, Moraes’ implication in the scandal gave Bolsonaro’s campaign enough ammunition to play into one of their most-used cards: that the left, and anyone associated with it, is corrupt – although Flávio Bolsonaro himself is also under investigation over alleged ties to the same bank. That comes as Lula’s own son, known as Lulinha, is separately under investigation for suspected influence-peddling. Pressure is also coming from outside Brazil, as Lula clashes with the Trump administration over tariffs and trading practices, Brazil’s resources, its view on organized crime and even scrutiny over its technology payment system, PIX. Trump has imposed new tariffs on Brazilian goods this year, including a 25% levy on some products over what the US described as unfair trade practices. Lula has rejected the allegations while continuing negotiations with Washington, and has increasingly made the defense of Brazilian sovereignty a central point of his campaign. “Brazil doesn’t fit in nobody’s backyard,” he told the UN General Assembly in September. That comes as Lula tightens ties with China and other BRICS members: Brazil’s exports to China reached $58.3 billion in the first half of 2026, more than triple the $17.4 billion sent to the US, whose share fell 13% as tariffs bit. Closer to home, Lula has also found himself at odds with a Latin America shifting to the right. In July, Argentina’s President Javier Milei flew to Brazil to campaign alongside Flávio Bolsonaro, calling Lula a “convict” and his government “thieving socialists” — prompting Brazil to recall its ambassador from Argentina. In Brazil, Lula also faces fading support even among parts of his base as the economic backdrop looks different from the one that accompanied his first presidency. His first two terms saw a global commodities boom that helped fuel growth, wages and employment in Brazil. Today, despite low unemployment and easing inflation, frustration over everyday expenses is weighing on voter’s perception of the economy — and weakening Lula’s support. Another Lula term would come at a moment of heightened rivalry between the US and China, Brazil’s largest trading partner, as well as wars and instability in Europe and the Middle East and growing tensions over global trade. A party built around an irreplaceable politician But even a PT victory won’t delay a problem the left has faced for some time: there is no clear successor to Lula. For younger Brazilians, French says, Lula has simply always been there. “He’s part of nature,” John French said. His raspy voice, his beard, his missing finger and the cadence of his speech have been fixtures of Brazilian public life since Brazil’s first direct presidential election after the dictatorship ended in 1985. He also created an emotional connection with voters who climbed the social ladder during the Lula years – a legacy that may be difficult to replicate. “His greatest achievement is social inclusion,” French said. “For people who were completely outside the labor market, outside the financial system, who didn’t even have bank accounts.” Kotscho agrees. “A guy like Lula, you don’t create, he’s unique,” Kotscho said. “These types only appear every 100 years.” Whether that’s enough to survive one more election — against a Bolsonaro, a banking scandal, and a region turning against him — is what Brazil might answer on Sunday. .

articles.summary: A Utah Supreme Court appeal in the Gabby Petito wrongful death case could clear the way for Charlie Kirk's family to sue over security failures.
articles.body: PROVO, Utah — A Utah Supreme Court battle stemming from Gabby Petito's 2021 murder could "pave the way" for Charlie Kirk's family to pursue a wrongful death lawsuit over alleged security failures surrounding his assassination at a Turning Point USA event last year, according to an attorney involved in the appeal. "Right now, Kirk's claims, if filed, would likely be dismissed, like Gabby Petito's claims were dismissed on that basis," said Brian Stewart, an attorney for the family of Gabby Petito who is working on the appeal involving their own wrongful death claim in the Beehive State. "We would need the Utah Supreme Court to overturn Tiede to pave the way for Charlie Kirk's family to proceed." articles.title: New York couple married in 1993 and ran several businesses; after divorce, a judge awarded the wife $6.83 million, including shares of company interests and payments, and an appeals court has now upheld the deal
articles.summary: A New York couple who married in 1993 and operated several businesses during their marriage have had their divorce-related property settlement upheld by
articles.body: A New York couple who married in 1993 and operated several businesses during their marriage have had their divorce-related property settlement upheld by an appeals court. On October 22, 2026, the New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Third Department, affirmed a judgment awarding Shirley F. Atkins $6,833,448 from the marital estate following her divorce from James C. Atkins. According to the court’s decision in Atkins v. Atkins, published by Justia, the award included a share of the husband’s interest in Northline Ventures, a utility construction business, payments from a stock sale and interests in two other companies. Both spouses had challenged aspects of the distribution.How the couple’s business interests became part of the divorceJames and Shirley Atkins married in 1993 and have two adult children. During their marriage, they owned and operated several businesses before eventually forming Northline Ventures, Inc., a utility construction company that James solely owned until 2020. That year, he redeemed 20% of his shares in the company in exchange for a promissory note worth $5,394,463, carrying 6% interest and payable in 80 quarterly instalments of $116,241. Northline Ventures subsequently sold those shares to an employee stock ownership plan, or ESOP. The payments due to James under the arrangement later became a point of contention in the divorce proceedings.James filed for divorce in January 2022, and Shirley subsequently filed her own claims for divorce and related relief. The couple reached agreements on most property-distribution issues, but several questions remained unresolved and proceeded to trial. In December 2024, a trial court in Clinton County determined that Shirley was entitled to 22.5% of James’s ownership interest in Northline Ventures, 22.5% of the quarterly payments arising from the stock sale and 22.5% of the value of his partial interests in Wild Goose Club, Inc., and SS & J Northeast Development, LLC. Together, these awards amounted to $6.83 million.Why the wife received a 22.5% shareBoth spouses challenged the percentage awarded to Shirley. She argued that she should receive 50% of James’s interest in Northline Ventures, while he maintained that her share should be limited to 10%. The appeals court rejected both arguments, finding that the trial court had appropriately considered the circumstances of the marriage and the parties’ contributions.The judges noted that Shirley had contributed directly to Northline Ventures between 2009 and 2014. She had also played substantial roles in the couple’s other businesses and projects while serving as the primary caretaker for their children. However, the court also considered Shirley’s acknowledgement that the construction company’s success was largely attributable to James’s vision and work. Its most profitable years came after her direct involvement had ended, and the evidence did not establish that its subsequent increase in value resulted from her indirect contributions.The court therefore found no reason to disturb the 22.5% award. It also upheld her share of the stock-sale payments, noting that the payments represented compensation for marital property sold during the marriage.How the $6.83 million award will be paidThe trial court directed James to make an initial payment of $1 million towards Shirley’s award. The remaining balance, slightly more than $5.8 million, was to be paid in quarterly instalments of $150,000, with 5% interest until the amount was fully paid. Shirley challenged the 5% rate, arguing that the balance should carry the statutory interest rate of 9%. The appeals court rejected her argument.It found that the trial court had considered the quarterly payments James received from the ESOP arrangement, the overall division of marital assets and evidence that Northline Ventures was not readily liquidated without financial and tax consequences. The judges concluded that the payment schedule and interest rate fell within the trial court’s discretion to determine a fair and equitable method of distributing marital property.Why the tax dispute did not change the outcomeJames also sought credit for paying Shirley’s share of the couple’s 2022 joint income tax liability. The couple had filed jointly, saving more than $130,000 in taxes. However, the court noted that Northline Ventures was an S corporation, meaning its income was reported as James’s income for tax purposes. Given the disparity in their reported incomes, much of the tax saving benefited James or the business.Shirley had also testified that the company had historically paid additional taxes owed by the couple, and James failed to establish that he had personally paid any part of her tax obligation. The appeals court therefore upheld the refusal to grant him a credit. The judgment was affirmed without costs. The decision reinforces that equitable distribution does not automatically mean an equal split, with courts weighing the length of a marriage, contributions to a business, caregiving responsibilities and the practical consequences of dividing assets.You use AI every day. articles.title: Malawi opposition demands answers over President Peter Mutharika's prolonged stay in South Africa
articles.summary: This is President Peter Mutharika's fifth visit to South Africa this year.
articles.body:
Malawi's opposition has demanded an explanation for President Peter Mutharika's prolonged stay in South Africa, as the country struggles with fuel shortages, power cuts and economic difficulties.

The 86-year-old Mutharika left Malawi on 6 October, for what officials described as a private visit. This is his fifth visit this year, with limited information made public on each of these trips.

"Malawi is at a critical moment, and there is a need for decisive action," the opposition Malawi Congress Party (MCP) said.

Information Minister Shadric Namalomba has denied that Mutharika's absence had created a leadership vacuum.

The professor who beat fraud allegations to become Malawi's president…again

Mutharika returned to power in October last year after defeating then-president Lazarus Chakwera.

He previously governed Malawi between 2014 and 2020.

His latest absence comes amid growing public scrutiny of his frequent visits to South Africa.

On Thursday, MCP campaign director Moses Kunkuyu told journalists in the capital, Lilongwe, that the opposition was not questioning the president's right to travel for personal reasons but wanted Vice-President Jane Ansah to address the nation over the country's mounting challenges.

He said that Malawians deserved to know who was managing the country's affairs.

"The issue is not that the president has traveled," he said. "The issue is that people are suffering and want reassurance that somebody is in charge."

He called on the government to explain how it intended to address persistent fuel shortages, frequent electricity blackouts, shortage of essential medicines in public hospitals and difficulties accessing foreign currency.

The information minister responded by telling local media that "a state president is always in charge at any time, anywhere," insisting that the president remained firmly in control of government affairs.

Asked about the purpose of the visit, the minister said: "A private trip is private."

He accused the opposition of attempting to exploit problems he said had developed under its previous administration.

"That is why Malawians voted us into government, not them. May I request them to seal their mouths as we address the problems they miserably created and failed to solve," he added.

On Thursday, Mutharika delegated the trade minister to lead Malawi's delegation to the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (Comesa) summit in Zimbabwe.

Earlier this month, officials dismissed reports on social media that Mutharika had travelled from South Africa to India for medical treatment.

Chief Secretary to the Government Justin Saidi said the president remained in South Africa and urged the public not to spread unverified information.

Mutharika has previously dismissed speculation about his health, describing such claims as "silly and laughable" and insisting that he was well.

Malawi faces a severe shortage of foreign currency, which has disrupted fuel imports and contributed to rising transport costs.

Long queues have formed at petrol stations, while unreliable electricity supplies and shortages of medicines have added to public frustration.

articles.title: Defense attorneys in Charlie Kirk's killing say they need several years to prepare for trial
articles.summary: Defense attorneys for the man accused of assassinating conservative activist Charlie Kirk are suggesting a 2029 trial date because they say it could take them that long to prepare their case.
articles.body: Defense attorneys for the man accused of assassinating conservative activist Charlie Kirk are suggesting a 2029 trial date because they say it could take them that long to prepare their case. Attorneys for Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, said Thursday that the defense's proposed schedule was “absurd” and defendant Tyler Robinson was simply trying to delay. Utah District Court Judge Tony Graf has scheduled a Friday hearing to set a trial date. Robinson pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in last year's killing of Kirk while the ally of President Donald Trump spoke to a crowd of several thousand people at Utah Valley University. The 23-year-old defendant turned himself in a day after the shooting, and his lawyers have not offered alternative theories for Kirk’s death. He could be eligible for the death penalty if convicted. Prosecutors from Utah County in court filings anticipated a 17-week trial and said they would be ready by October 2027. But rather than hold the proceedings during the Thanksgiving and Christmas holidays, they proposed the trial begin Jan. 31, 2028. Erika Kirk’s attorney, Jeffrey Neiman, said the trial should start next October, the earliest date identified by prosecutors. “Under the Defendants’ proposed schedule, Mr. Kirk’s two children, who were one and three at the time he was murdered, will be six and eight years old by the time the trial concludes,” Neiman wrote. “They will face the uncertainty of this criminal proceeding longer than they had their father in their lives.” But Robinson's attorneys said in court filings this week that they must sift through tens of thousands of files turned over by prosecutors. They said they'll have to conduct extensive investigations into Robinson's life in search of mitigating factors that could influence his sentence if convicted, and must devote “substantial time” to issues such as jury selection. The defense lawyers said they respected the court's attempt to set a “realistic trial date.” Yet because it's a complex death penalty case, trying to predict when it will be ready for trial “is an exercise that, at this time, will necessarily be infected with false precision,” they wrote in a document filed Wednesday.

articles.title: Washington parents find their courage as girls walk off cross country course in protest of trans runner
articles.summary: Over 100 adults rallied outside a Camas High girls cross country district meet to protest a biological male competitor as Initiative 638 looms.
articles.body: CAMAS, Wash. — The sign seemed innocuous enough. So did the man holding it. But a passing jogger apparently saw things differently. Outside a district cross country meet in which a biological male was competing against girls, Steve Lynch held a sign that read: "Coached X-C & Track for 24 years. If you have questions about the differences between Girls & Boys...answers given here FREE of charge!" But as Lynch began explaining those differences, the jogger shouted: "Jesus loves a firing squad! Go kill Muslims! Go kill trans people! That's your rhetoric, right? F--- you!" DAD BANNED FROM SCHOOL GROUNDS AFTER PROTESTING TRANS RUNNER COMPETING AGAINST HIS DAUGHTER Lynch didn't even flinch. In fact, he smiled. "Oftentimes I have to deal with that," he said. Lynch represents courage on this issue, which is something many adults lack. Over the past few weeks, it's been mostly students, not grown-ups, who have led the opposition to a Camas High cross country runner competing against girls after starting the season on the boys team. But a rally outside Wednesday's meet — where the boy finished second among a field of 25 to help lead Camas to the girls district championship — showed that the adults are catching up in the bravery department. PARENTS SPEAK OUT ON THE INGRAHAM ANGLE AFTER GIRLS FORFEIT RACE OVER BIOLOGICAL MALE RUNNER There looked to be more than 100 grown-ups, maybe 200, in attendance — mostly dressed in garb advocating for the separation of males and females in sports. At the heart of the rally was Initiative 638 — a Nov. 3 ballot measure in Washington state that would enforce such separation in K-12 athletics. People such as Sarah Burns, the mother of a Camas runner who walked off the start line in protest last week, never imagined herself playing the role of activist when the cross country season began. But now she finds herself at the center of one of the most contentious debates in Washington state. "I was just a mom going to watch her daughter, and then we found out what was happening, and I couldn't not say something," said Burns, wearing an XX-XY Athletics shirt. "These are teenage girls that should be able to be teenage girls and run and compete in their sport and not have their achievements taken from them." Burns was not the only Camas parent willing to speak out on Wednesday. Also in attendance was Sarah Babb, whose daughter Madeline walked off the start line last week as well. Like Burns' daughter, Holly, Madeline had no idea her actions would prompt such widespread media attention. But as reporters from across the nation showed up to cover Wednesday's rally and meet, Sarah was no longer feeling quite so isolated. "As a mom who comes to these races all season long, it feels very alone as I stand there and go, 'This is awful,'" Babb said. "So it was great to see such support last week, and this is wild this week. It's hard to be the quiet majority, to feel like we're being bullied into silence. I think a lot of people feel that way. I know it's scary. It's scary." It certainly can be. Over the past couple weeks that I've been covering this story, most parents have been reluctant to speak — even anonymously. Many have expressed fear of losing their jobs, and one even said, "I don't want my house burned down." It's easy to catastrophize, especially when you see how vicious opponents of the Protect Women's Sports crowd can be. There was the aforementioned jogger. There was the Golden State Valkyries fan who told an XX-XY shirt-wearer to "f---ing kill yourself" at a WNBA Finals game last week. There was the Seattle Storm co-owner telling a girl with the same shirt that she's "f---ing insane" in July, bringing that girl to tears. WASHINGTON HIGH SCHOOL GIRL WALKS OFF STARTING LINE ALONE IN PROTEST OF TRANS RUNNER, ENDING HER SEASON Surely one can see why parents would want to sit this issue out, right? Women's sports advocate Amy Sousa isn't so sure. "I don't have a lot of patience for adults who are willing to let the girls take the hits," Sousa said. "If these girls are willing to stand up to their peers, I think adults can stand up to theirs. And if they can't do it in public, at least they can do it at the ballot." There were some people at Wednesday's rally very much against I-638. One was a woman named Stephanie, who didn't want her last name used but was cordial with me and my photographer. She said the measure would require invasive genital exams to prove one's sex, which is not true. When I mentioned that there were other options such as cheek swabs, she argued that that would be too expensive and that there weren't enough trans athletes for such testing to be worthwhile. When I mentioned all the female athletes speaking out against having to compete against biological males as a matter of fairness, she offered the following: "Fairness is reasonable, and I do think there should be rules. Even in the Olympics, each sport can set up certain rules. I don't want to wrestle with somebody who's got 40 pounds on me, whether they're male or female," Stephanie said. "But that's about size, not just about what gender you're born." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Come on, though. It's more than about size, isn't it? How many women under 6'4" have you seen dunk a basketball? Yet there are countless men under that height who can. Biology matters in every sport. In fact, it was a difference in biology that ultimately led Camas High senior Kate Westfall — the fastest girl on the cross country roster — to quit the team earlier in the month. Westfall won districts last year. She had bigger aspirations in her final high school season. But she walked away from it all because she felt racing against a boy simply wasn't fair. So Wednesday, her parents — Joe and Jennie — showed up to districts in protect-women's-sports attire to honor their daughter's courage. "She made the brave decision to forgo the rest of her senior season and give up opportunities in order to bring awareness to the impact the current state policy is having on females who are being forced to compete in this unfair environment," Jennie said. "As her parents, we are proud of her courage and are honored to stand with her." OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD Jennie and Joe admit to a fear of backlash. But that's the thing about courage — without fear, it doesn't exist.

Here’s what to know today. Trump promised $2 gas and cheaper groceries. Here’s what voters got instead. When voters headed to the polls nearly two years ago, Donald Trump promised them cheaper groceries, gas below $2 a gallon and a wave of new manufacturing jobs. They elected him president — and got the opposite. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. Instead, prices have kept rising and wages have struggled to keep pace with inflation. While the broader economy has grown at a healthy rate, the gains have disproportionately flowed to the wealthiest households. Economists largely point to Trump’s own policies for his broken campaign promises. Take cheaper groceries. Prices are up 3.5% from January 2025, when Trump came into office, in part because of tariffs and higher fuel costs following the Iran war. Speaking of fuel, Trump promised gas for $2 a gallon. But the national average of regular gas is $4.27, according to AAA — the first time gas has ever averaged more than $4 a gallon in October. Taxes, however, are lower on average, as Trump promised. And while tax law partially achieves his pledge to eliminate taxes on tips and overtime, the reality is a little more complicated. Read the full analysis here. Rallying this week in Greenville, North Carolina, Trump said Republican Michael Whatley was going to lose to Democratic challenger Roy Cooper in their Senate race. Whatley cruised to primary victory as Trump’s handpicked candidate for the seat held by retiring Sen. Thom Tillis. But he has struggled to overcome a number of disadvantages. Democratic challenger Roy Cooper is relatively popular in the state after two successful bids for governor and has fundraised millions more than Whatley. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray on Friday accused the BJP of "murdering" democracy by allegedly exerting pressure on the media and using religious polarisation to divert public attention. The barb came after an audio clip triggered a political row over claims of a Rs 500 crore payment to Maratha quota activist Manoj Jarange.In a post on X, Thackeray said the 29-minute recording, which has gone viral in Maharashtra, allegedly featured BJP office-bearers, a senior Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) functionary and social media influencers discussing political strategies, media pressure and ways to divert attention from sensitive issues by fuelling religious polarisation.“The chief minister has tried to buy time by saying he’s called for a forensic report on the audio clip, making a show of justice,” Thackeray said, referring to Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis's announcement of a forensic examination.“But if you actually listen to the conversation in this, you’ll realize it’s nothing short of a murder and rape of democracy itself!” he added.Thackeray said the alleged Rs 500 crore payment mentioned in the recording required an explanation but argued that the broader allegations about attempts to influence the media and public discourse also deserved scrutiny. He urged Fadnavis to investigate the conversations allegedly captured in the clip, rather than limiting the inquiry to verifying the recording's authenticity.The controversy erupted after Jarange released a portion of the recording on Thursday, alleging a conspiracy to silence him and weaken his agitation for Maratha reservation. In one segment, a woman allegedly claims that Rs 500 crore had been delivered to Jarange through Shiv Sena MP Shrikant Shinde, son of deputy chief minister Eknath Shinde.The recording also purportedly contains discussions about Jarange's growing political influence ahead of the 2024 Maharashtra assembly elections and strategies to counter his agitation in the Marathwada region.Fadnavis has said the audio clips and conversations would undergo a thorough forensic examination. Shiv Sena leaders have also sought an investigation, while BJP leaders have questioned the recording's authenticity and the timing of its release. articles.title: France tightens security in anticipation of weekend protests
articles.summary: Gatherings banned and curfews extended as cities lock down in an effort to avert further unrest.
articles.body:
French authorities have announced tightened security measures in a bid to prevent a repeat of violent unrest during protests last weekend.

President Emmanuel Macron was due to hold a meeting on Friday with his defence council, made up of top ministers and officials, and to meet security forces, as cities across the country confirmed limits on gatherings and public transport.

Macron’s announcement on Thursday that only union demonstrations would be authorised at the weekend has prompted harsh criticism from student groups whose demonstrations in recent weeks against conditions in schools were joined by groups denouncing high living costs and other grievances.

More than half a million people gathered across France last Saturday for demonstrations that spiralled into violence and looting.

Paris has extended a nighttime curfew until Monday, while Marseille and Lyon have banned gatherings, introduced curfews, and restricted public transport for this coming Saturday.

Police deployments will also be increased by 20 percent compared with last weekend, after the government was accused of being blindsided by the scale of the unrest.

Macron, who has blamed “seditious” ultra-left groups for the unrest, is due to announce “additional decisions” following the defence council meeting, his office said.

Despite the restrictions, France’s main student union, UNEF, has called ⁠⁠for rallies on Saturday. The Yellow Vest movement, an anti-establishment force that first emerged in 2018 and re-entered the French political consciousness last weekend, has filed plans for a march through central Paris.

Macron was due to meet student representatives later on Friday to discuss their plans, but UNEF said their rallies would go ahead.

“Macron is trampling upon the freedom to protest in our country, and is spitting on the values of the republic he claims to defend,” UNEF said.

Shops and businesses in major cities have been urged to close. The Louvre and the Louis Vuitton Foundation will be closed on Saturday, while the Paris edition of the Art Basel fair will end on Friday, two days ahead of schedule.

Since last Saturday’s violence, 2,700 people have been arrested, according to the Ministry of Justice.

articles.title: Meghan ‘deeply distressed’ by report alleging her dad possessed child sexual abuse images
articles.summary: Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, said Friday that she was “deeply distressed” by allegations that her dad Thomas Markle possessed child sexual abuse images.
articles.body: LONDON — Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, said Friday that she was “deeply distressed” by a report alleging that her estranged father, Thomas Markle, possessed child sexual abuse images, and said that she was informed by police of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018. In a statement on Friday, Meghan addressed the report that her father was being investigated over claims he kept child sexual abuse images at his home in the Philippines. The allegations were first reported by The Sun newspaper, a British tabloid, which reported that Markle’s son had informed police after finding finding a hoard of images. The Sun published a photo it said showed Markle’s son, Thomas Jr., as signing a sworn statement it said he had submitted to police and quoted Markle Jr. as saying: “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.” Thomas Markle Sr. denied the reported allegations, calling them “sick lies” in a statement to Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper. He added they were “the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.” NBC News was not immediately able to identify a contact for Markle Sr., 82, who the Daily Mail reported was now in a Florida rehab center recovering from surgery. Police in Cebu City, the location of Markle Sr.’s home in the Philippines, and London’s Metropolitan Police did not immediately respond to a request for comment from NBC News. Meghan has long had a limited and fraught relationship with her father, who did not attend her wedding to Prince Harry in 2018. Thomas Markle Sr. married Meghan’s mother, Doria Ragland, in 1979 and they subsequently divorced in 1987. In the rare statement on Friday, Meghan said that she had chosen to keep her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, away from her father “for one reason: to protect them.” “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed,” she said in the statement. Meghan said that she had been made aware of a letter sent to the British police and other authorities in 2018, that “made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.” “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them,” she said. “Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children,” Meghan added. Asked by NBC News when Meghan was made aware of the letter to the Metropolitan Police, a spokesman for the couple said it was in the summer of 2018 after her wedding with Prince Harry. Meghan, 45, and Harry, 42, moved back to the United Kingdom earlier this summer after several years in the United States. The couple made their first joint public appearance last week visiting charities in central England. King Charles III has made clear that their return does not signal a return to active royal life. Prince Harry, however, has said recently he wants his disagreements with his family to “work out.”

articles.title: US tourist in Italy falls 1,000 feet to death on mountain hike
articles.summary: A Florida woman died after plunging more than 300 meters (around 1,000 feet) while hiking in the Italian Dolomite mountains, according to police in the northern city of Trentino.
articles.body: A Florida woman died after plunging more than 300 meters (around 1,000 feet) while hiking in the Italian Dolomite mountains, according to police in the northern city of Trentino. Her death on Saturday was announced late this week after her next of kin were notified, police say. Michelle Alejandra Rubio-Leiva, who was 36 and from Miami, was on vacation with family members on the Forcella Pordoi trail, a high-altitude site in the Sella group of the Dolomites, when she fell, police told CNN. The UNESCO World Heritage Site, known for its sweeping views and zig-zag canyon, is only accessible by cable car and reaches 2,848 meters (9,344 feet) at its highest. Rubio-Leiva’s sister, who was with her at the time, alerted emergency services, which dispatched a team of specialists from the Trentino Alpine and Cave Rescue Services and a rescue helicopter to descend to the spot from where her body was eventually recovered. The two women had left the trail to reach a steep exposed spot on an upper cliff to take a picture when Rubio-Leiva slipped and fell into the canyon below, according to emergency workers who described the accident to local media. Rubio-Leiva’s family members were airlifted to Canazei while her body was retrieved, the local carabinieri told CNN. The recovery operation lasted several hours. The hiking area is extremely dangerous and known for steep inclines, loose gravel and falling rocks, according to the Italian Alpine Rescue unit, which told CNN that more than 80 people died in the Dolomites in 2026 so far.

articles.title: Are parents in France and Italy liable for damage caused by student protesters?
articles.summary: Parents could face financial penalties if their children participate in vandalism or looting during demonstrations.
articles.body:
As high school student protests began in France last month, footage soon spread on social media of angry parents dragging their children away from demonstrations.

They may have good reason for doing so as France considers plans to impose fines on those whose children vandalise or damage property following a similar measure introduced this week in Italy.

As young protesters across France were joined by others angry about the rising cost of living and proposed public spending cuts, similar youth-led demonstrations have begun in Italian cities. Many have turned violent with protesters burning barricades, and police accused of using excessive force.

What are the protests in France and Italy about?

In late September, high school students in the northern Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis began protesting about the state of their school buildings and teacher shortages. They were particularly angry about the proposed government budget which includes millions of euros in cuts to public spending.

Students in Paris, and later in other French cities, erected barricades around their schools and caused hundreds of closures during the first week of October.

Later, the protests spread nationwide as public sector workers joined demonstrations to oppose planned pay freezes. Now the protests have widened again , with those angry about the rising cost of living, petrol shortages and fuel prices joining demonstrations which have frequently descended into rioting, looting and arson.

French President Emmanuel Macron said last week that “nothing justifies” violence and that local officials could ban certain street gatherings if deemed necessary. French authorities also announced curfews .

But last Saturday, hundreds of thousands of protesters in France, Italy, Spain, Belgium and Portugal took part in largely uncoordinated demonstrations against rising living costs.

Initially peaceful weekend protests in Milan descended into riots, with groups of mainly young people looting shops, smashing windows and clashing with police. Masked protesters threw stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and set fire to barricades made from bar tables.

Riots were also reported in the Italian cities of Bologna and Turin.

Official figures on the expected costs of the damage in both France and Italy have yet to be established.

On Tuesday, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government approved a series of measures in response to the unrest, including sending 500 soldiers to Milan until the end of the year and increasing financial liability on parents whose children were involved in vandalism and looting.

Under new rules, anyone taking part in a group of at least five people and endangering public safety during protests faces up to five years in prison and a maximum fine of 20,000 euros ($22,460).

Protesters aged 14 to 18 can now be subject to administrative detention, even if they have not committed a crime, provided there is evidence that they pose a danger, extending powers that previously applied only to adults.

In part of the decree, which includes the phrase “You break it, you buy it”, Italy also strengthened the law holding parents responsible for criminal damage by their children.

Article 2048 of the civil code already states that parents and guardians are liable for damages caused by the “unlawful act of unemancipated minor children or persons subject to guardianship who live with them. The same provision applies to the foster parent”.

In Italy, authorities may enforce these laws through asset and wage attachments.

The new measure permits the state to directly fine parents or claim damages for any resulting loss against parents’ property or by deducting public subsidies the family receives.

Under article 1242 of the French Civil Code, parents who live with their children and exercise parental authority also have a civil liability for damage that their children cause.

“Parents, in their capacity as holders of parental authority, are by right jointly and severally liable for damage caused by their minor children, except when the latter have been entrusted to a third party by an administrative or judicial decision,” the law states.

Last year, a new law amended article 1242 to strengthen parents’ role during youth justice proceedings. It removed the cohabitation requirement for parents for civil liability to apply.

In France, compensation from parents for damage caused by children can be enforced through civil proceedings, and can include the seizure of assets if not covered by civil liability insurance, which is often tied to housing insurance, subject to the terms of the policy agreement.

On Friday, French radio station RFI reported that a new bill known as “rioters pay” is now also being proposed by the government in response to the violent protests.

The government is scheduled to debate the draft bill on October 27.

If the law is passed, those found responsible for vandalism could be required to pay up to 10,000 euros ($11,200) in compensation. In the case of criminal damage by minors, parents could be held responsible.

A provision to the bill could also introduce collective civil liability, potentially requiring someone in a group responsible for damage to pay, even if they did not cause it themselves, on the same financial terms as those who caused the damage, RFI reported.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu described the legislation as “absolutely essential” to ensure taxpayers do not pay for damage caused by protests.

Several other countries also hold parents financially liable for damages their children cause.

For example, in Sweden, parents or legal guardians may be held financially liable, subject to statutory conditions and limits, for certain injuries or property damage caused by a child who commits a crime.

In the United States, subject to state-specific conditions and limits, laws addressing parental responsibility specify that if a minor intentionally destroys public property, businesses, or vehicles, victims or local government can sue the parents in civil court.

articles.title: At least 7 people killed in shooting at church in Jordan, public security agency says
articles.summary: At least seven people were killed after gunmen opened fire inside a church in Jordan’s Karak province 90 miles south of the capital Amman, Jordan’s public security agency said.
articles.body: At least seven people were killed after gunmen opened fire inside a church in Jordan’s Karak province 90 miles south of the capital Amman, Jordan’s public security agency said. “Security forces are following up on an incident of gunfire in Karak Governorate,” Jordan’s government spokesperson Mohammad Al-Momani wrote on X. The “unidentified” gunmen are being pursued, the security agency said, adding that the shooting happened during a funeral. A witness told state-run Al-Mamlaka television that one attacker was carrying an AK-47 Kalashnikov rifle, and the shooting continued for several minutes. The incident took place in Hmood, a predominantly Christian town in northern Karak. “Some guys were standing outside the church before two people got out of a vehicle and started shooting,” Tamer Halsa, an eyewitness told Al-Mamlaka television. Dozens were believed to be inside the church, witnesses told state media. “We were more than 150 people inside and outside the church,” Halsa added. This story is breaking and will be updated.

articles.title: October full Moon: How and when to see the Hunter's Moon
articles.summary: October's full Moon, known as the Hunter's Moon, will rise on Sunday night. Will the weather be in your favour?
articles.body:
October's full Moon, nicknamed the Hunter's Moon, is set to light up the night sky this weekend.

It will be visible in the UK from Sunday 25 October into the morning of Monday 26 October.

Marking the 11th full Moon of 13 in 2026, it is the final one before a run of four consecutive supermoons , external .

If you want to catch a glimpse, keep an eye on the forecast to see if the weather will allow a clear view.

When is the best time to view the Hunter's Moon?

The Moon will rise in the east at just after 16:00 GMT on Sunday and set towards the west between 07:00 and 08:00 GMT on Monday - times vary across the UK.

The Moon will be officially full at 04:11 GMT on Monday. This is the moment of "syzygy" when the Sun and Moon will be aligned either side of the Earth.

However, the Moon will appear full on both Sunday and Monday nights, giving skygazers two chances to spot it.

During a full Moon, the whole of the Earth-facing side of the Moon is illuminated by the Sun.

You may notice an orange or reddish hue to the Moon when it is low in the sky due to the scattering of short wavelength blue light as it passes through a large depth of the atmosphere.

The longer wavelength red and orange colours are not scattered as readily so pass through to our eyes.

The Moon may also appear larger in the sky near moonrise and moonset - something called the "Moon Illusion".

This is when our brain makes us think the Moon looks bigger because it is viewed alongside objects on the horizon such as buildings and trees.

As well as looking out for the full Moon, there is also a chance to spot some shooting stars, with the Orionid meteor shower just past its peak.

The extra lunar light, however, may obscure some of the meteors, so be patient and leave time for your eyes to adjust.

Full Moons throughout the year have traditionally been given names that reflect what is going on in nature .

Different cultures use different names for the 12 or 13 full Moons across the lunar calendar, but many of the common ones we use today originate from Native American cultures.

In October, the term Hunter's Moon comes from the time of year hunters would have been most active, preparing for the colder and darker winter months ahead.

The Hunter's Moon is known to sit in the sky for a particularly long time - similar to the preceding Harvest Moon - giving hunters extra light in the skies.

Will the weather be clear enough to see the Moon?

Storm Boelo will continue to bring rain and very strong winds to northern Scotland early on Sunday night, but prospects of seeing the Moon increases as the night wears on.

There will be plenty of blustery showers in west Scotland and north-west England - any gaps between these could give a brief chance to view.

For the rest of the UK prospects are better, especially early in the night with clearer skies, before cloud tends to spread in from the south-west later.

If the weather fails to cooperate where you live, the next chance to see a full Moon will be on 24 November as the Beaver Supermoon.

This will be followed by a Christmas Eve Cold Supermoon on 24 December.

The succession of supermoons will then continue into 2027, with January and February's full Moons both set to be supermoons too.
