articles.title: Fifty Antifa groups in France join vast network to ensure chaos in weekend protests
articles.summary: A Fox News Digital investigation identified 50 militant Antifa cells mobilizing protesters to descend on Orléans for the National Rally congress.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Some 50 radical Antifa cells in a wider network of nearly 300 groups are mobilizing to ensure this weekend's demonstrations in France devolve into chaos and mayhem, Fox News Digital has learned. Self-described Antifa groups are working with a sprawling network of communist, socialist, far-left and anti-Israel groups to mobilize on two fronts this weekend: an "anti-fascist village" against conservative leader Marine Le Pen's National Rally in the city of Orléans and nationwide protests called Acte II to replicate last week's violent riots. A Fox News Digital investigation has mapped 287 groups in France's expanding protest ecosystem, including 50 explicitly Antifa organizations, 27 explicitly communist, socialist, Trotskyist or revolutionary-left organizations, 24 labor unions and an expanding coalition of far-left anti-Israel, migrant-rights, environmental, feminist, transgender and other activist organizations. The demonstrations, which claim to be about youth education, include just 27 student and youth organizations. The coordination comes amid a wider transnational campaign of mayhem organized by communist, socialist and leftist groups in Greece, Italy, Spain, India and elsewhere. Fox News Digital has compiled a running who's who of organizations in what has been dubbed "Chaos Inc." and will keep updating the directory. The size of the mobilization represents a huge expansion from the original 54 organizations identified in last weekend's riots. The number of Acte II actions has also increased to 649 planned protests, as of early Friday morning in Paris, including at 21 train stations, three ports, two oil depots and one refinery. Scores of pages of planning documents and social media posts analyzed by Fox News Digital reveal that agitators have laid the groundwork for a coordinated campaign with money, logistics and a communications infrastructure behind their efforts. The fundraising, transportation, youth outreach, ready-made materials and centralized information hub reveal an organized mobilization operation in place days before protesters even reach the streets with expected hammer-and-sickle and Palestinian flags. A French administrative court reportedly overturned a ban on street protests issued by Paris police, although the order was not made public and it was unclear if it would have applied to other cities which have imposed similar orders. Already, organizers have begun planning a next-stage Acte III on Oct. 31, a broader strike and blockade mobilization on Nov. 5 and a Europe-wide action on Nov. 20. In France, the numbers include signatories to two streams: a Ciao Fachos, or "Good-bye Fascists," coalition that will descend on Orléans and the Acte II, or "Action 2," campaign, led by a group called the Yellow Vests that organized last week's mayhem. Organizations have signed onto a roster and list headed to Orléans. "Macron must leave and make way for the people!" the Acte II organizers declared, calling "Yellow vests, high school students, university students, workers" into "demonstrations, roundabouts and blockades, everywhere in France." FRANCE'S MACRON BLAMES PROTESTS ON 'ULTRA-LEFT GROUPS WHOSE AIM IS TO BRING DOWN THE REPUBLIC' Last September, after the murder of conservative leader Charlie Kirk by an alleged leftist gunman, President Donald Trump issued an executive order that designated Antifa as a domestic terrorist organization. Soon after, Trump issued National Security Presidential Memorandum 7, targeting far-left groups. It said the "groups and entities that perpetuate this extremism have created a movement that embraces and elevates violence to achieve policy outcomes, including justifying additional assassinations." Despite the clear global presence of groups with self-described names of Antifa, former FBI Director Christopher Wray told Congress in 2020 that Antifa was "not a group or an organization" but rather "a movement or an ideology." In the U.S., while they will wave flags that say "ANTIFASCIST," far-left activists don't typically operate under one formal national organization called "Antifa," leading to denials that any "Antifa" organization exists. In Europe, it's a different story. Activists openly organize under the Antifa name, "antifascist" banners and Antifa flags with emblems of their local chapters, and a Fox News Digital investigation has found a sprawling network mobilizing activists for another weekend of protests. Last November, the State Department designated four European groups linked to Antifa — Antifa Ost in Germany; the International Revolutionary Front, or Informal Anarchist Federation, in Italy; and Armed Proletarian Justice and Revolutionary Class Self Defense in Greece — as Foreign Terrorist Organizations and Specifically Designated Global Terrorists, accusing them of organizing or carrying out bombings, shootings and other politically motivated attacks. TRUMP CALLS ANTIFA ‘TERRORIST GROUP,’ FUELING FIGHT OVER FREE SPEECH AND LIMITS OF LAW ENFORCEMENT Worldwide, Antifa chapters have built their movement around a seemingly noble opposition to "fascism," but critics argue that they deploy tactics of threats, intimidation, harassment, violence, destruction and even murder that make them coercive, authoritarian, dangerous and deadly. What's more, parroting the propaganda language of Russia, China and the Islamic Republic of Iran, "fascism" has become a loaded catch-all phrase to describe Western democracies. For example, late last year, Neville Roy Singham, an American-born communist tech tycoon living in China, took to the stage at the Golden Tulip Hotel in Shanghai for a "Global South" conference and critiqued the alleged "fascism" of the United States. Days ago, Fox News Digital reported exclusively that an internal State Department assessment warns that antifascist groups could participate in a "potentially more confrontational protest" this weekend that could "expose further security shortcomings and deepen political tensions." Now, the organizations themselves provide a look inside the infrastructure being assembled on the ground. Free Buses to the "Antifascist Village" On Friday night, a bus is set to leave Marseille at about 9 p.m. local time for Orléans, in a journey organized by "La Riposte Antifasciste Marseille," established in October 2023 with a "strategy of massification of anti-fascism." In its promotion, the pilgrimage leaders tell followers, "Anti-fascism is everyone's business." It's joined by Marseille Unite Communiste Libertaire. Other organizing materials advertise collective transportation from locations including Paris, Saint-Denis, Stains and Brest. The logistical preparations provide a more concrete measure of organization than simply finding similar flags or slogans at demonstrations. On Saturday morning, at 8 a.m., in the city of Bagnolet outside Paris, the Assemblée Antifasciste de Bagnolet, or "Bagnolet Antifascist Assembly" has plans in place to meet at the town hall, Mairie de Bagnolet, on Rue Hoche for a two-hour ride to Orléans. Its online sign-up sheet advertises 50 free seats. La Marche des Solidarites, or "The March for Solidarity," an online hub, directs supporters in the Paris region to buses leaving from Saturday morning from Place de la République in Saint-Denis and Stains with #NousToutes and Carré Citoyen. On Instagram, Saint-Denis Antifa, Carre Citoyen and Marche des Solidarites are sending people to a fundraising page on the Solidaire website, where organizers have raised about $13,300 for expenses for the Saturday action, including the "printing of mobilization materials: leaflets, posters, etc." and a "truck/sound system for a large procession of the solidarity march." The Saint-Denis Antifa also made crêpes last week at the Saint-Denis Hip-Hop Festival to raise money for the protest. And organizers have centralized the machinery for mobilization online. Adults are facilitating space for high-school students, telling them, "free places are for you." The Marche des Solidarités online repository on antiracisme-solidarite.org describes itself as a place containing "all the information to mobilize," including "calls, signatories, visuals, etc." Ciao Fachos has gone further. Its organizing documents call for "tractages, collages, réunions publiques, récoltes de fonds, transports collectifs" — distributing leaflets, putting up posters, holding public meetings, fundraising and organizing collective transportation. The group also urges activists to prevent National Rally supporters from distributing literature at markets or putting posters on walls. The network has also advertised Signal channels, much like far-left activists have done in the U.S., to swap information and coordinate logistics. COULD FRANCE'S RIOTS HAPPEN HERE? EXPERTS SEE PARALLELS IN SOCIALISM, IMMIGRATION — AND KEY DIFFERENCES A Two-Day Orléans Antifa Operation The schedule is carefully organized with Antifa groups like Loiret Antifasciste, which is promoting a detailed program. The group's own declaration describes the objective as larger than opposing a single National Rally convention. Building a "mouvement antifasciste," or "antifascist movement," is a "collective responsibility," the organization says, calling for a united political front. For Saturday, organizers advertise: On Sunday, Ciao Fachos advertised another demonstration toward CO'Met, the location of the National Rally gathering. The Association France Palestine Solidarité says its members will participate in a Palestinian contingent during Saturday's demonstration and operate a stand at the antifascist village until 10 p.m. Protest leaders chose the last protest date of Oct. 17 to memorialize a protest on the same day in 1961 when a protest by Algerian "martyrs" turned deadly in Paris. Organizations include Urgence Palestine Orléans, AGIR POUR LA PALESTINE, Union juive française pour la paix, migrant-rights organizations including FASTI, Droits Devant!!, Coordination Sans-Papiers 75, La Cimade Aix-en-Provence, Tous Réfugiés, GASPROM-ASTI Nantes, ASTI Orléans, the Association des Travailleurs Maghrébins de France and UJFP, the French Jewish Union for Peace, which is promoting the demonstration. The CGT Paris, the Paris branch of one of France's largest labor confederations, is also organizing transportation to the demonstration and published the Loiret Antifaciste coalition's call for an antifascist movement. Solidaires 37, the Indre-et-Loire branch of the left-wing labor federation, is organizing pay-what-you-can transportation from Tours. The coalition lists demonstrate how explicitly antifascist organizations operate inside a considerably larger political coalition. Antifa Joins 'Acte II' The Orléans demonstration isn't the only place explicit Antifa organizations are mobilizing Saturday. Fox News Digital separately identified antifascist groups attached directly to local Acte II demonstrations. In Angoulême, Action Antifasciste 16, also known as Action AntiFa16, appears as an official collaborator on an Oct. 24 Acte II announcement alongside NPA Charente, Révolution Permanente Angoulême, Maison des Peuples et de la Paix, Fanfare en lutte d'Angoulême and Organisation de Solidarité Trans Angoulême. In the city of Caen, the "Caen Antifa Squad" appears as a collaborator on another announcement explicitly advertising "ACTE II — 24 OCTOBRE." The presence of Antifa groups provides a connective point between the nationwide Yellow Vest mobilization and the antifascist ecosystem. One of the figures attempting to bring the different grievances together is Benjamin Ball, editor of the website coordinating the Yellow Vest action map. "Our role is to make sure that the social anger aggregates," Ball recently told French media, saying organizers want representatives of different sectors received at the Élysée. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: FRANCE BRACES FOR MORE UNREST AFTER PARTS OF PARIS SPUN OUT OF CONTROL Communists, Socialists and Antifa French Antifa activism substantially overlaps with anarchist, communist, anticapitalist and revolutionary-socialist networks whose organizations frequently cooperate in demonstrations and campaigns. The Oct. 24 coalition illustrates those connections. Union Communiste Libertaire, a libertarian-communist organization advocating revolutionary political change, has joined the mobilization. The revolutionary socialist Nouveau Parti anticapitaliste, or NPA, is promoting the Orléans demonstration. Its publication "L'Anticapitaliste" reported that dozens of organizations were mobilizing against the RN congress. La France Insoumise, the French Communist Party, Union pour la Reconstruction Communiste and Le Poing Levé appear in the wider local coalition. The coalition also includes labor organizations, environmental activists and student groups, such as Fédération Syndicale Étudiante, a left-wing student union already involved in France's October student revolt, is joining the mobilization. Extinction Rebellion France is represented through its Île-de-France organization. Its agitators rappelled the Marianne statue and hoisted a vest with an anti-police message, creating the iconic image used for the next phase of activation. And the coalition includes feminist organizations such as NousToutes, whose current social-media material is promoting transportation to Orléans and mobilization resources. Labor Unions Move Activists to Orléans with Antifa Organized labor is providing another piece of the mobilization infrastructure. Along with CGT Paris and Solidaires 37, the expanded roster includes CNT Fédération Éducation, CNT 49, CNT Education 93, SNETAP-FSU, Solidaires 44, Solidaires 35, SUD Protection Sociale 93 and CGT ArianeGroup Issac, among other labor organizations. VISA 93, part of the Vigilance et Initiatives Syndicales Antifascistes labor-antifascist network, has promoted union transportation for the demonstration. Meanwhile, as Antifa and other leftist agitators readied for the weekend, French authorities arrested a 34-year-old man, Hodei Docampo Ciarra, this week in the town of Val d'Issoire (Haute-Vienne). Police suspect him of being one of the rioters who devastated City Hall in Limoges, torching the building. French police said he was allegedly involved in the "ultra-left." articles.title: Bridgwater Airbnb host fined as guests put at 'serious' risk
articles.summary: The company was fined £52,000 and ordered to pay £2,000 surcharge.
articles.body:
An Airbnb host has been fined £52,000 after admitting seven fire safety offences that put guests at "serious" risk.

Following an inspection in August 2024, owners of Walpole House in Bridgwater were temporarily banned from renting out the accommodation to guests after inspectors found there were no fire doors, fire alarms or evacuation procedures in place.

These deficiencies raised "significant concerns about the safety of people sleeping at the premises", inspectors said.

Fire safety inspector Tony Hickey said the consequences of inadequate fire safety can be "devastating", adding: "The failures identified in this case were serious."

Walpole House Limited was sentenced at Taunton Magistrates' Court on Monday after pleading guilty to seven offences under the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005.

The company was fined £52,000 and ordered to pay a £2,000 surcharge and prosecution costs of £9,801.

Michael George Krishnan, one of the directors of Walpole House, who also operated a separate sole-trader business providing sleeping accommodation at the premises, was prosecuted separately.

He was fined £1,480 and ordered to pay a £592 surcharge. He also pleaded guilty to seven offences under the fire safety order.

Hickey investigated the case on behalf of Devon and Somerset Fire and Rescue Service after the issue came to light following a referral from the local council.

The accommodation deficiencies meant guest lacked adequate warning of a fire and abilities to escape safely, inspectors added.

Hickey continued: "Fire safety is not optional. Anyone providing sleeping accommodation has a legal responsibility to ensure that appropriate fire safety measures are in place to protect the lives of those staying at their premises."

Airtel’s pack asks for Rs 41 over the prepaid price and adds 30GB of data plus the wider OTT bundle. For anyone already paying YouTube directly, that gap is easy to justify.Airtel is pitching the bundle around how people now spend their mobile data: following creators, catching up on shows and streaming music. Adding YouTube to a pack already heavy on streaming services brings creator content and music into the same recharge.Claiming YouTube Premium takes a few taps in the Airtel appOnce the top-up is purchased, users need to open the Airtel app, head to the ‘Rewards & OTTs’ section and claim YouTube Premium from there.The subscription runs only as long as the top-up. articles.title: Govt to expand emergency ambulance services through app-based aggregators
articles.summary: Bihar govt plans to expand emergency ambulance services via app-based aggregators like Ola, Uber and Rapido; firms asked to submit reports and ensure compliance.
articles.body: Patna: The state govt is planning to expand emergency ambulance services through app-based transport aggregators, including Ola, Uber, Rapido and Sawari Mithila, to improve passenger convenience and access to emergency transportation. The companies have been directed to submit reports on the proposed services within a week, transport department secretary Raj Kumar said on Friday.The directions were issued during a review meeting at the transport department headquarters with representatives of the aggregator companies. The meeting assessed compliance with earlier instructions issued following discussions with app-based service providers and motor cab drivers’ associations.The department has also asked the companies to introduce chatbot facilities in Hindi and English to help passengers and drivers access information and resolve service-related problems. Aggregators have been asked to establish call-support systems to address drivers’ complaints promptly and ensure that only eligible commercial vehicles are attached to their platforms.Officials also reviewed provisions relating to night charges, ride-cancellation fees, passenger information and broadcasting systems. The companies have been asked to increase the duration of broadcast messages from two seconds to 10 seconds so users can understand the information.“The department has identified eight major areas requiring compliance. These include establishing local offices in Bihar, providing call support for drivers, offering bilingual chatbots, extending broadcast message duration, ensuring clarity on night and cancellation charges, preparing a standard operating procedure (SOP) for driver ID suspension, attaching only commercial vehicles and arranging designated parking facilities for aggregator vehicles at airports,” Raj Kumar said.The proposed SOP for suspending driver IDs is intended to ensure adherence to the principles of natural justice. Companies have also been asked to complete the process of signing a memorandum of understanding with the Airport Authority to identify suitable parking areas for their vehicles.During the review, Raj Kumar examined compliance reports submitted by the companies. Ola and Uber were issued show-cause notices and directed to submit compliance reports by Oct 30, 2026.“App-based transport services must operate in accordance with prescribed rules. The directions were aimed at improving passenger services, resolving drivers’ grievances and ensuring greater transparency in operations. All companies must comply within the stipulated deadlines,” Raj Kumar said.State transport commissioner Arif Ahsan said special attention was being given to passenger convenience, drivers’ concerns and regulatory compliance.“Officials have been instructed to monitor implementation, verify compliance where necessary and take appropriate action. articles.title: France students' unrest: 70,000 police deployed, Paris museums closed ahead of fresh weekend protests
articles.summary: French authorities announced the deployment of around 70,000 law enforcement personnel, including gendarmes (military police), as the country braced for
articles.body: French authorities announced the deployment of around 70,000 law enforcement personnel, including gendarmes (military police), as the country braced for potential violence during another weekend of student-led protests.According to French interior minister Laurent Nuñez, who announced the security measures, elite police units would help protect public buildings, including city halls, after rioters set fire to the historic Limoges City Hall, a 143-year-old building, on October 17.“There have been numerous calls from radical far-left groups on social media to commit acts of violence and vandalism. There have also been renewed calls for looting, with those messages clearly being spread by rioters,” Nuñez told reporters at a news conference in Paris on Friday.“We will be absolutely uncompromising with those involved in violence. Police will have a very firm approach to making arrests, and there will be legal consequences,” he added.His statement came after protests last week descended into violence, with demonstrators setting fires, storming public buildings, smashing shop windows, looting and clashing with police, marking France’s worst unrest in years.Demonstrators are now planning to take to the streets again on Saturday to protest the rising cost of living. Students, members of the CGT labour union and activists from the “Yellow Vest” movement, whose protests against social injustice shook France in 2018 and 2019, are expected to join the demonstrations.Paris museums to remain closedMeanwhile, France’s culture ministry announced the closure of several prominent museums in Paris.In a statement to The Associated Press, the ministry confirmed that the Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums, along with the Grand Palais, would remain closed. It also urged all institutions under its authority to take the necessary measures to ensure “visitor safety, staff protection and the preservation of artworks”.After two days of invitation-only admission, Art Basel Paris opened to the public on Friday, but only for the day, as fears of unrest prompted organisers to cancel the weekend programme. One of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, Art Basel features exhibitions by 211 international galleries at Paris’ Grand Palais.“This decision has not been taken lightly, and the safety of everyone involved in the fair remains our utmost priority,” organisers stated on Thursday.You use AI every day. articles.title: Trump ordered to testify in $10bn BBC lawsuit discovery: What happens now?
articles.summary: Trump could face sanctions, including dismissal of his lawsuit, if he fails to cooperate with questioning.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump must answer questions under oath in the discovery stage of his $10bn lawsuit against the BBC, a federal judge has ruled, warning that failure to cooperate could lead to the dismissal of his case.

The dispute centres on a BBC documentary which combined separate excerpts from a speech he gave before the January 6, 2021 attack on the US Capitol.

The broadcaster has apologised for the edit but denies that Trump has grounds for a defamation claim. Here is what the ruling means and how the case reached this point.

Trump has been ordered to make himself available for questioning by the BBC’s lawyers by December 11, unless the judge overseeing the case extends the time frame for gathering evidence. That process is currently scheduled to end on December 18.

The ruling comes after the president’s legal team sought to postpone questioning until January. Judge Enjolique Lett also rejected his lawyers’ attempt to prevent the session from being filmed. Access to the recording will initially be restricted to lawyers involved in the case.

Separately, she gave Trump’s side 30 days to hand over relevant documents requested by the BBC.

A deposition is a formal interview under oath, usually conducted outside the courtroom before a trial. Lawyers question a witness and the answers are recorded in a transcript. The testimony can later be used in court, including to challenge a witness whose account changes.

It forms part of “discovery” – the stage of a US civil lawsuit in which both sides are given time to obtain relevant evidence through examining documents, submitting written questions and taking witness testimony. The process allows each side to examine the other’s claims and prepare its case.

Trump’s deposition is expected to last up to seven hours.

Trump filed his lawsuit against the British broadcaster in federal court in Florida on December 15, 2025, over a Panorama documentary which was broadcast shortly before the 2024 US presidential election.

His complaint seeks at least $5bn for alleged defamation and another $5bn for alleged violations of Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. He alleges that the programme damaged his reputation and business interests by falsely portraying him as directly encouraging violence at the Capitol.

The BBC, which has apologised for the way the programme was edited, however, disputes those allegations and has sought to have the case dismissed. It also challenges the Florida court’s jurisdiction, arguing that the documentary was produced in London and was never broadcast in the US.

Trump’s lawyers contend that viewers in Florida could have accessed the programme through BritBox or by using a virtual private network (VPN), which can disguise a user’s location. The BBC says the documentary was not available on BritBox International or its international website.

The documentary combined remarks from separate sections of Trump’s January 6 speech into what appeared to be a continuous statement: “We’re going to walk down to the Capitol and I’ll be there with you… And we fight. We fight like hell and if you don’t fight like hell, you’re not going to have a country anymore.”

Two quotes that make up the excerpt used by the BBC were delivered roughly 54 minutes apart. The programme also left out his appeal for supporters to “peacefully and patriotically make your voices heard”, Trump’s lawyers say.

The BBC acknowledged that the edit created the mistaken impression that Trump had made a direct call for violent action. It apologised, while rejecting his demand for compensation and denying a legal basis for the defamation claim.

The controversy was followed by the resignations of BBC director-general Tim Davie and its news chief, Deborah Turness.

Trump has also suggested, without evidence, that artificial intelligence was used to put words into his speech.

Trump had agreed to be questioned on October 16, but his lawyers cancelled that date, citing a matter of national importance.

Trump’s lawyers subsequently proposed dates between January 11 and 22 of next year.

At Thursday’s hearing, BBC lawyer Charles Tobin said Trump had instead been campaigning in Georgia and asked the court to compel Trump to attend the deposition sooner, arguing that waiting until January would push the questioning beyond the existing deadline for gathering evidence.

Lett upheld the BBC’s complaint that Trump’s team had been too slow to hand over internal documents. Charles Tobin, on behalf of the BBC, told the Miami court: “We still have a completely lopsided [situation] here on discovery. They have produced absolutely nothing of any substance”.

Lett warned that failure to cooperate could lead to sanctions, including dismissal of the lawsuit altogether. That would mean Trump’s own attempt to recover damages could end because he would have failed to fulfil his obligations as the person bringing the case.

Under federal civil procedure rules, discovery sanctions can also include ordering a party to pay legal expenses caused by noncompliance, preventing it from introducing certain evidence or striking out parts of its case. These are possible penalties, rather than sanctions already imposed on Trump.
